% 4. REPLACEMENT PARAGRAPHS FOR SECTION 5 (Mechanistic analysis)
%    Replaces the four \paragraph blocks currently in that section.
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\paragraph{The direction controls refusal, but not uniformly by ablation:} Adding $\hat{r}$
drives benign refusal from near zero to $100\%$ in every model, reproducing the additive half
of \citet{arditi2024refusal} on each architecture. Ablation is less uniform. It lowers the
harmful refusal rate in Mistral ($46\%\to34\%$), Llama ($71\%\to59\%$) and Command-R
($67\%\to34\%$), but in Qwen ($78\%\to92\%$) and Gemma ($65\%\to100\%$) it
\emph{raises} measured refusal. Inspecting the generations shows why: ablation shifts the
phrasing of the refusal rather than removing it, out of the first-person modal forms
(``I cannot\ldots'') and into constructions like ``Certainly not. Submitting a client trade
without proper approval is a serious violation.'' A regex classifier keyed to the former reads
that shift as a behavioural drop; a classifier that reads the whole response does not. We
therefore report ablation under the same three-way classifier used for
Table~\ref{tab:headline-divergence}. The auto-selected layers sit in the upper-middle part of
each network, and the addition coefficient spans more than three orders of magnitude, from
$29.8$ in Mistral to roughly $75{,}800$ in Gemma.

\paragraph{Tool context suppresses the refusal signal:} For our harmful triples, the mean
refusal activation drops significantly from no-tool to tool-enabled modes in four of the five
models (Table~\ref{tab:mech}, with $t = 5.6$ for Qwen, $t = 5.1$ for Mistral, $t = 9.7$ for
Command-R, and $t = 4.0$ for Gemma, but null for Llama at $t = 0.4$; Figure~\ref{fig:proj}).
Whether tools rotate the direction or merely attenuate it varies by family
(Table~\ref{tab:cosine}). In Qwen, Mistral and Gemma the text- and tool-derived directions stay
closely aligned ($0.74$--$0.80$), consistent with attenuation along a shared axis. In Command-R
($0.39$) and Llama ($0.21$) the alignment is much weaker, so for those two the shared-axis
reading is not supported by our measurements. Llama is also the model where suppression is null,
making it the clearest case in which tool context relates to the refusal representation
differently than in the other families.

\paragraph{The refusal direction is a strong predictor but a partial mediator:} A lower refusal
activation reliably predicts an unsafe call in every model, with AUC from $0.76$ to
$0.86$ under the global-scope tool-call scorer. At the same time, when we patch a
tool run's projection back to its no-tool level, only a fraction of the unsafe calls revert to
being safe: 18 percent for Qwen and 24 percent for Mistral. The refusal direction is therefore a
partial mediator of the transfer failure, not a complete account of it. The unrecovered portion
may reflect an incomplete one-dimensional intervention, refusal may be represented across
additional directions, other layers, or other token positions, or nonlinear and distributed
mechanisms that a single-scalar patch does not restore. Our design also varies tool availability
jointly with tool-oriented prompt wording, so we cannot attribute the remaining failures to tool
affordance specifically; we can only conclude that restoring this one signal is not sufficient as
a control mechanism. The balance between the two varies by model. For Command-R, for example, the
affordance mediates much more strongly than the others at 62 percent, although only on a smaller
unsafe set.

\paragraph{The direction gates engagement, not the safety of the action:} To test whether the
direction controls behaviour and not only wording, we ablate it on harmful tool-enabled prompts
and score the unsafe tool call directly, a predicate over the parsed calls that involves no
refusal classifier (Table~\ref{tab:ablation-action}). The headline unsafe rate moves in both
directions across families. What is consistent is the rate conditional on the model having called
a tool at all, which barely moves anywhere ($0.78\to0.64$, $0.77\to0.75$, $0.89\to0.78$,
$0.61\to0.64$), while the rate of calling a tool at all swings by 10 to 22 points and in both
directions. Ablation therefore changes how often a model engages, not how safely it acts once
engaged. Gemma is the limiting case: its tool-calling collapses to zero, so its apparent safety
gain is the model ceasing to act rather than acting safely, and is better read as capability
damage than as alignment.

\paragraph{Steering is a blunt lever:} When raising the steering coefficient, the harmful unsafe
rate does decrease towards zero, but the benign over-refusal rate rises accordingly
(Figure~\ref{fig:steer}). For Qwen, removing unsafe calls entirely costs $44$ percent
benign over-refusal; in Command-R, Gemma and Llama the same operating point costs essentially all
benign tool use. No coefficient in our grid removes unsafe behaviour without large collateral
over-refusal. Steering through the refusal direction is therefore an imprecise safety control.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
% 5. REPLACEMENT for the Section 3.6 'Robustness of the direction' paragraph
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

\paragraph{Robustness of the direction:} Our refusal direction contrasts across request type,
subtracting activations for harmful and benign prompts. To verify that the result is not an
artifact of that choice, we additionally extract a behaviour-defined direction, taking the
difference in means between refused and complied harmful prompts, and measure its cosine
similarity with the request-type direction (Table~\ref{tab:cosine}). The two are closely aligned
in every model ($0.69$--$0.86$), confirming that request harmfulness and the refusal decision
occupy substantially the same axis. Because models rarely comply with harmful requests, the
complied side is small (as few as 25 per class in Gemma); folding hedged compliance in with
compliance roughly doubles it and moves the cosine by at most $0.04$. Recomputing the
behaviour-defined direction under the previous refusal labels agrees with the current one at
$0.96$--$0.98$ in every model, so this check does not depend on the relabelling.

% 6. METHODS ADDITIONS (reproducibility; Section 3.5 / 3.6)
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

% Append to \subsection{Refusal classification}:
All interventions in Section~\ref{sec:mech} are scored with this same classifier. This matters
for the intervention results specifically: a regex classifier keyed to first-person refusal
phrasing misreads ablation, which changes how a model refuses, as a change in whether it refuses.

% Append to \subsection{Mechanistic methods}:
\paragraph{Prompt construction under tools:} Chat templates differ in whether they can carry tool
definitions. Passing tools to a template with no tool-handling block silently drops them, turning
a tool-enabled prompt into a plain chat prompt and making every response score as safe. Gemma-3
has no tool-handling block in any published checkpoint, so for that model we write the tool
schemas into the prompt text; this reconstruction gives a $12.5\%$ unsafe rate on harmful
tool-normal prompts against $14.6\%$ from the behavioural run, and reproduces its published AUC
to within $0.001$. We verify for every model that a tool name appears in the rendered prompt
before running any tool-mode measurement. Llama-3.1-70B weights were loaded from a bf16 mirror
(\texttt{unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct}) whose chat template carries tools; an otherwise
identical mirror ships a stripped template that does not.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
% 7. DISCUSSION FIX
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
% The paragraph 'A shared refusal direction, suppressed rather than replaced' currently asserts
% that ablations collapse refusal in all models and that text- and tool-derived directions are
% aligned. Both need softening. Suggested replacement for its first half:

We find that the single refusal direction \citet{arditi2024refusal} identify for chat refusal is
present in all five models we probe: additions induce benign over-refusal everywhere, and the
behaviour-defined and request-type directions are closely aligned (Table~\ref{tab:cosine}).
Ablation, however, reduces refusal in only three of the five, and in two it changes the wording of
refusal rather than its presence. Where tool context does suppress the signal it does so along a
largely shared axis in Qwen, Mistral and Gemma, though not in Command-R or Llama. The divergence
is therefore better described as attenuation of an existing safety representation in most
families than as a separate tool-mode circuit, consistent with evidence that text safety
alignment is often shallow~\citep{qi2024safety}.
